segments.narration: Four people broke into the Pantheon to repair its clock. Paris, the mid-2000s. Nobody hired them, and nobody asked.
Its clock had sat dead since the 1960s. So they built a workshop up under the dome and worked there for about a year.
One of them, Jean-Baptiste Viot, was a professional clockmaker. He took the mechanism apart piece by piece. Who breaks in to do unpaid maintenance?
They call themselves Untergunther, part of a Paris underground network that quietly restores neglected heritage. When the clock ran again, they went and told the management themselves.
France took them to court for it. The judge ruled in their favour in about twenty minutes, and years later Viot won the official contract to restore the same clock.

verdicts.claim: Members of a clandestine group entered the Pantheon in Paris without permission to restore its clock; the project became public in 2007.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia dates the project becoming public to October 2007 and the news report to late November 2007; because no source checked gives the start year, the narration says 'the mid-2000s' rather than naming one.
